title: Unbundling the database: dataflow apps and streaming databases
goal: By the end you can show that an index, a replica and a view are each built by snapshot plus catch-up from one log, tell federation from unbundling, decide what work goes on the write path and what on the read path, push a view's changes to clients that resume from an offset, and make a read wait for its own write.

warmup.q: A merchant taps "refund 30.00". The API appends the refund to the log and returns 201. The app at once re-reads the merchant's balance from a read model that a stream job keeps up to date from that log. What does the merchant see?
options: Always the new balance, because the write returned 201
Sometimes the old balance, because the stream job may not have applied the refund yet
An error, because the read model is locked while the job updates it
Always the new balance, because a Kafka topic is strongly consistent
warmup.why: 201 means the log has the refund. The read model is derived from the log and applies it on its next poll, some milliseconds later. A read in between gets the old balance. In this lesson's Try it, with a 50 ms poll, 331 of 1,000 such reads are stale. The first option is the trap: on a single database the write and the read hit the same store, so read-your-writes comes free, and it's easy to assume a derived store behaves the same way. The log being consistent doesn't help, because the read doesn't go to the log.

sections.h: A database already builds its indexes and replicas from one log
sections.body:
Inside PostgreSQL, every change is written to the write-ahead log first (the Storage engines track's lesson on the WAL). Several structures are kept in step with the table. An index is a sorted copy of one column with pointers back to the rows. A streaming replica is a second server that replays the same WAL (the Replication track's lesson on replication logs). A materialized view is a stored query result (the Storage engines track's lesson on materialized views). Each is derived data. The database maintains all of them inside one process, and a commit makes the row and its index entries visible together. That's why nobody calls an index eventually consistent.

Now build an index on a table that is taking writes. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` can't lock the table for the minutes the build takes, so PostgreSQL does it in phases, and the Try it watches them through the `pg_stat_progress_create_index` view. First it scans the table as of a snapshot, 3,000,001 rows in the Try it, sorts the entries and loads them into a new index. Meanwhile an insert loop added 139 more rows, which the snapshot didn't contain. So it scans again, compares the index with the table, and adds what's missing. Only then does it mark the index valid. A query afterwards finds all 1,640 rows for one merchant, including the ones written during the build.

That is three steps: snapshot, catch up on the writes since, then keep up. You've seen them before. A new streaming replica copies the data files with `pg_basebackup` and then replays WAL from the position where the copy began (the Replication track's lesson on PostgreSQL replication). Debezium takes an initial snapshot of each table, then streams changes from its replication slot (the Stream processing track's lesson on change data capture). And lesson 1's kappa replay started a new job at offset 0, caught up, and kept up. Inside a database or outside it, a derived structure is built and maintained the same way.

In a 2014 Strange Loop talk, "Turning the database inside-out with Apache Samza", Martin Kleppmann asked what happens if you take this machinery out of the database. Make the log, Kafka in his talk, the system's main write path. Then build every read-optimized structure (indexes, caches, materialized views) as a stream processor consuming that log. A cache built this way is a view that keeps itself current, with none of the invalidation code the Caching track's lesson on invalidation had to get right. The figure shows the two shapes side by side. Taking the database apart this way is called **unbundling** it.

try.title: Watch CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY snapshot and catch up
steps: From the `labs` folder, start PostgreSQL 18 with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, then open three terminals with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.

In the second, start a stream of live writes: `INSERT INTO derive_payments (merchant, amount_cents) VALUES ('m-0042', 1234) \watch 0.05`. In the third, watch progress: `SELECT phase, blocks_done, blocks_total, tuples_done, tuples_total FROM pg_stat_progress_create_index \watch 0.1`.

Back in the first: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY derive_payments_merchant ON derive_payments (merchant);`. When it finishes, stop the inserts (Ctrl+C) and run `SELECT count(*) FROM derive_payments WHERE merchant = 'm-0042';`. Predict the count before you run it: the table had 1,500 rows for m-0042 before the inserts began.

code.title: three psql sessions
code.src:
-- session 2: live writes, 20 a second
INSERT INTO derive_payments (merchant, amount_cents) VALUES ('m-0042', 1234) \watch 0.05

-- session 3: the build's progress
SELECT phase, blocks_done, blocks_total, tuples_done, tuples_total
FROM pg_stat_progress_create_index \watch 0.1

-- session 1: the build
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY derive_payments_merchant ON derive_payments (merchant);

try.expect:
The first row of each phase, from this run (your block and tuple counts differ with timing, and a fast laptop may skip past a short phase between two refreshes):
```text
 phase                                   | blocks_done | blocks_total | tuples_done | tuples_total
 building index: scanning table          |           0 |            0 |           0 |            0
 building index: sorting live tuples     |       19109 |        19109 |           0 |            0
 building index: loading tuples in tree  |           0 |            0 |      646057 |      3000001
 index validation: scanning index        |         686 |         2682 |           0 |            0
 index validation: scanning table        |        6979 |        19110 |           0 |            0
```
The build loaded exactly the 3,000,001 rows in its snapshot (one insert landed before it). The two validation phases are the catch-up: they compare the index with the table and add the rows inserted during the build. The final count was 1,640 in this run, 1,500 old rows plus 140 inserts, and `EXPLAIN` shows it answered by an `Index Only Scan using derive_payments_merchant`. Your count depends on how long your inserts ran, and the index has every one of them.

sections.h: Federation unifies reads; unbundling unifies writes
sections.body:
There are two ways to make five stores feel like one database, and they solve different problems.

The first is **federation**: one query interface over many engines. Trino (the Batch track's lesson on choosing an engine) joins a PostgreSQL table with an Iceberg table in one SQL statement. PostgreSQL's `postgres_fdw` makes a table on another server look local. Federation answers questions that span stores. It does nothing to keep them in agreement: if OpenSearch is missing 40 payments that PostgreSQL has, a federated query happily returns both versions.

The second, **unbundling**, keeps the writes in agreement. One log carries every change, CDC or an outbox feeds it, and each derived store has a consumer that applies the changes in log order. This is the harder problem, which is why most of Part IV was about it: ordering, crashes between a write and an offset commit, replays when code changes. Across products built by different teams there is no transaction that spans them all. Kafka's exactly-once covers only Kafka (the Messaging track's lesson on exactly-once), and two-phase commit across products is the XA that most teams avoid. An ordered log with idempotent consumers is the tool that works.

What runs in those consumers is your code, and that's the point. The search document for a payment needs the merchant's trading name and the issuing country of the card's BIN, joined in and normalized. A fraud feature is a windowed sum. These are derivation functions, and they are ordinary application logic. A database offers triggers and stored procedures for this, but code inside the database sits outside your build, your tests, your rolling deploys and your monitoring. In a dataflow app the derivation is a Kotlin service, versioned and deployed like every other.

The same thinking changes how services talk. The fraud scorer today calls the merchant-risk service for every payment: 20 ms typically, 120 ms at p99, and when the risk service is down, scoring fails. Instead, the scorer can consume the topic of risk-tier changes and keep its own local table. The lookup takes microseconds and survives a risk-service outage, though the tier it reads may be a few seconds old. One RPC per request has become a stream-table join, which the Stream processing track built with Kafka Streams.

Unbundling isn't free. Kafka, Debezium, a stream processor and two more stores mean five systems to learn, upgrade and watch. Its value is breadth, joining stores that each do one thing well. If one product does everything you need, use the one product.

try.title: Federation, unbundling, or just one database
steps: For each need below, choose federation, unbundling (log plus consumers), or one database, and give the reason in one line.

1. Finance wants one ad hoc query joining last month's PostgreSQL disputes with the Iceberg settlement history. 2. Support's search must show a refund within a few seconds of it being issued. 3. A new internal tool for 12 staff needs users, roles and a list of tickets. 4. The fraud scorer must stop calling the merchant-risk service on every payment. 5. The data team wants to explore whether a Redis cache and PostgreSQL disagree. 6. A new recommendations store must be rebuilt every time its model changes.
try.expect: 1. Federation: a read across two stores, once; Trino or a foreign table answers it without moving data. 2. Unbundling: the index must follow every write, in order, so feed it from the change log. 3. One database: PostgreSQL does all of it, and five systems would be cost with no benefit. 4. Unbundling: consume the risk-tier topic into a local table, a stream-table join. 5. Federation, as a diagnostic: one query can show both copies side by side; it won't fix them, and the fix is a rebuild from the log. 6. Unbundling: a derived store with a replayable source can be rebuilt with lesson 1's recipe whenever the derivation changes.

sections.h: Work on the write path or the read path, and push changes to the screen
sections.body:
Every derived dataset splits work between two moments. The **write path** is work done when data arrives, eagerly, whether or not anyone asks. The **read path** is work done when someone asks. The derived dataset is where the two meet.

Take the merchant dashboard's "takings today". With no derived data, every refresh runs `SUM(amount)` over the merchant's payments: nothing on the write path, everything on the read path. With an index on `(merchant, created_at)`, the write path maintains the index and the read path scans one merchant's rows for the day. With a maintained per-merchant total, the write path adds each payment to a counter and the read path is one lookup. Each step moves work earlier: reads get cheaper and writes get dearer. You can't precompute every possible question, since 2,000 merchants times every date range and filter is far too many, so you precompute the questions that are asked constantly and leave the rest to the read path.

Now follow the derived data one step further, onto the merchant's screen. The number on the dashboard is a copy of the server's view, and a copy that nobody updates goes stale. Polling keeps it fresh at a price. In the Try it, 2,000 dashboards polling every 5 seconds make 400 requests a second, 88% of the answers haven't changed, and the screen is still 2.67 seconds behind at the median. Pushing instead extends the write path to the client. When the view changes, the server sends a diff over a connection the client keeps open (Server-Sent Events or a WebSocket). That's 50 messages a second, one per change, and the screen trails the payment by 0.15 seconds.

A pushed diff has the problems of any log consumer, and the same fix. A phone that goes offline misses diffs. So each diff carries the log offset that caused it, the phone remembers the last offset it applied, and on reconnect it asks for everything after that offset. A diff is usually a delta ("-45.00"), and a delta applied twice is wrong, so the phone drops any diff whose offset isn't newer than its last. The stepper walks a single write all the way to the screen.

Sync engines package this, with the client's own writes added. The Replication track's local-first lesson took Zero (1.11.4) and ElectricSQL's client (1.5.28) apart. Convex (1.49.0) makes every query function a subscription: when the data a query read changes, Convex updates every subscribed client, all to the same database snapshot. You can also log reads as events, recording that a support agent saw balance 955.00 before approving a payout, which turns "what did they see?" into a lookup.

stepper.title: A write travels to the view, then to the screen
stepper.intro: One transfer of 45.00 from acc-01. The processor polls the log every 50 ms. The phone also shows acc-01's balance from pushed diffs.

frames.say: Later the phone loses its connection, and the diff for offset 42 (another 20.00) is lost on the way. On reconnect it asks the feed for acc-01's diffs **after 41** and applies 42. When a delayed live copy of 42 arrives too, its offset is not above 42, so the phone ignores it. A diff is a delta, so applying it twice would show 915.00.

try.title: Poll 2,000 dashboards, or push to them
steps: Run the demo. It sends ten minutes of payments, 50 a second, to 2,000 merchants, each with one dashboard open, and measures how long each screen shows an old total.
Predict for polling every 5 seconds: requests per second, and the share of answers that are unchanged.
Find the polling interval in the output that comes closest to push's staleness. What does it cost in requests?

code.title: PushVsPollDemo.kt (excerpt)

try.expect:
```text
                         msgs/s  answers unchanged    stale p50    stale p99
poll every 1 s            2,000              97.5%      0.64 s      1.15 s
poll every 5 s              400              88.2%      2.67 s      5.09 s
poll every 30 s              66              46.9%     15.12 s     29.84 s
push diffs                   50               0.0%      0.15 s      0.22 s
```
Polling costs requests in proportion to the number of screens, whether or not anything changed. Pushing costs messages in proportion to the number of changes. Even polling every second, 40 times the traffic, leaves the screen four times staler than pushing, and 97.5% of those requests carry nothing new. The price of pushing is an open connection per screen and the offset bookkeeping above.

sections.h: Streaming databases maintain the views for you, and they are still behind
sections.body:
Writing a consumer by hand for every view means getting joins, deletes and late data right each time. **Streaming databases** let you declare the view in SQL and maintain it incrementally, with the delta rules from the Storage engines track's lesson on materialized views, applied continuously to a change stream. Three are worth knowing in November 2026.

Materialize (v26.49.1, with roughly weekly releases) is built on differential dataflow. Its `SUBSCRIBE` statement turns a view into a stream: first the current rows, then every change as it happens. Each row comes with `mz_timestamp` and `mz_diff`, where +1 means a row was inserted and -1 that one was removed, so an update arrives as a -1 for the old row and a +1 for the new one. RisingWave (v3.1.1, Apache 2.0) keeps its state in an LSM tree on object storage. `CREATE SUBSCRIPTION` on a table or materialized view, read through a subscription cursor, gives the changes with an `op` column (Insert, Delete, UpdateInsert, UpdateDelete). Feldera (v0.379.0, still before 1.0, with almost daily releases) implements DBSP, the theory in Budiu and colleagues' VLDB 2023 best paper. Every change is a Z-set, a set of rows with integer weights (+1 or -1), and the engine works out, for each SQL operator, how an input delta becomes an output delta.

```sql
-- the dashboard's view, declared once; the engine keeps it current
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW merchant_takings AS
SELECT merchant_id, sum(amount_cents) AS takings_cents, count(*) AS payments
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'CAPTURED'
GROUP BY merchant_id;

SUBSCRIBE TO merchant_takings;   -- Materialize: current rows, then each change
```

That is unbundling packaged as a product: the change stream in, your query as the derivation function, diffs out to subscribers. It doesn't change the timing. A streaming database reads PostgreSQL's change stream asynchronously, so it is a derived copy like the hand-written consumer, and a merchant who refunds through PostgreSQL and reads `merchant_takings` a moment later can see the old total.

The fix is the lab's. The write path returns its position: a Kafka record's offset, or PostgreSQL's WAL position after the commit. The read says which position it needs and waits until the view has applied it. The Try it measures it. With the view polling every 50 ms, 331 of 1,000 reads right after the user's own write are stale. Waiting for the write's offset makes it 0. The wait is paid only by the reads that would have been stale, so the median wait is 0 ms and the 99th percentile is 37 ms. Make the view slower, polling every 200 ms, and 781 reads are stale, and the 99th percentile wait grows to 183 ms. Waiting removes stale reads; it can't hide a slow view.

try.title: Read your own write from a derived view
steps: Run the demo. It runs the lab's experiment at three poll intervals: 1,000 users each send a transfer and read their own balance 5 to 65 ms later, first from the view as it is, then waiting for their own offset.
Predict for the 50 ms poll: what share of the immediate reads are stale? A tenth, a third, or most?
Look at the waiting column. Why is the median wait 0 at 10 and 50 ms, but not at 200 ms?

code.title: StaleReadDemo.kt (excerpt)

try.expect:
```text
poll     read now                 read after my offset
10 ms    45 of 1,000 stale        0 stale, p50 0 ms, p99 5 ms
50 ms    331 of 1,000 stale       0 stale, p50 0 ms, p99 37 ms
200 ms   781 of 1,000 stale       0 stale, p50 63 ms, p99 183 ms
```
The stale share tracks how often a read lands between a write and the next poll. At 10 and 50 ms most reads arrive after the poll, so they don't wait at all. At 200 ms, 78% of reads arrive before it and every one of them waits, so the median moves up. These are the same 1,000 users as the lab's tests, which check the 331 exactly.

refs.title: Budiu et al., DBSP: Automatic Incremental View Maintenance for Rich Query Languages (PVLDB 16(7), 2023)

analogy: A newsroom and a wire service. Reporters file each story once, to the wire (the log). Every newspaper that subscribes runs its own desk: one cuts stories to 200 words, one translates them, one only keeps sport. Each paper is a derived view with its own editing code, and none of them blocks the wire if its desk is slow. A paper that's off the wire for a day asks for everything since its last story number. The analogy breaks at the reader: a newspaper reader expects yesterday's news, while your user who just filed the story expects to see it in the paper at once, and only waiting for its story number guarantees that.
in_your_world: Your Quarkus services probably already run a small version of this: a Kafka Streams or plain consumer that keeps a read model (a Redis hash of balances, an OpenSearch index of payments) up to date from a topic. Two habits make it honest. First, have the write endpoint return its position. That's Kafka's `RecordMetadata.offset()` after the send, or the database's log position after the commit when CDC feeds the read model (`pg_current_wal_lsn()` in PostgreSQL; Oracle calls its position the SCN). Then let a read that needs its own write pass that position and wait, with a timeout, until the read model's last applied position reaches it; every other read goes straight through. Second, when you push changes to a merchant portal over SSE, send the offset with every event and support `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect, which SSE clients send automatically, so a reconnecting browser resumes from the right place instead of reloading everything. A Temporal workflow that has to act on a derived view can use the same trick: carry the offset in the workflow input and wait for it in an activity.
mistake: The common mistake is treating a derived read model as if it were the database you wrote to: return 201 from the write, then read your own data back from the read model and show it as confirmed. It works in development, where the consumer is idle and applies each event within a millisecond, and fails in production under load, where the consumer is seconds behind. Users see their payment missing, retry, and pay twice. The fix is to decide per read. A read that must include the caller's own write either goes to the system of record, or carries the write's offset and waits for the read model to reach it. Every other read uses the read model as it is. A version of the same mistake is pushing diffs without offsets: after any reconnect, the client applies some deltas twice and shows a balance that no server ever had.

worked.title: Make a read wait for its own write

steps.say: **The write path returns a position.** The API appends to the log and hands the offset back to the client with the response, like an LSN.
steps.code: fun transfer(t: Transfer): Long = log.append(t)    // the offset of this write

steps.say: **The derivation function returns what it changed.** Applying an entry produces diffs that carry the entry's offset, so anyone downstream can tell old from new.
**A read that needs the write either goes now or parks.** If the view has applied the offset, answer at once. Otherwise remember the read.
**Each poll releases what it caught up with, once.** Remove the ready reads before answering them, so a reply that triggers more work can't answer the same read twice.
**The client applies pushed diffs once, in order.** Its last applied offset decides; the same rule makes reconnecting safe.

lab.title: A dataflow app that pushes diffs and reads its own writes
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 13 fail.

Read the comment at the top of `Dataflow.kt`: it maps the write path, the derivation, the read path and the push onto the classes. `Sim.kt` is virtual time, and `App.kt` wires everything together and runs the read-your-writes experiment.

Write `Balances.apply` (move the money, return the two diffs, payer first), `Feed.since` (a filter over the feed's history) and `ClientCopy.receive` in `Client.kt` (apply a diff only if its offset is above `lastOffset`, otherwise count it as ignored). The three `DataflowTest` tests for them pass.
Write `Processor.readAfter` and `releaseParked`. `poll` calls `releaseParked` after every poll, so every test that runs the app has been failing on its `TODO` until now.

Run all the tests. `ReadYourWritesTest` checks the exact numbers from this lesson's Try it: 331 stale reads without waiting, 0 with it, and a 99th-percentile wait of 37 ms. `PushTest` includes a client that reconnects and receives the same diff twice.
hints: `Balances.apply`: `balances.merge(t.from, -t.cents, Long::plus)` and the same with `+t.cents` for `t.to`, then `listOf(Diff(e.offset, t.from, -t.cents), Diff(e.offset, t.to, t.cents))`.
`Feed.since`: `history.filter { it.account == account && it.offset > afterOffset }`. The history is already in offset order.
`releaseParked`: take the ready ones with `parked.filter { it.offset <= applied }`, remove them with `parked.removeAll(ready)`, then call each `reply(readNow(it.account))`.
If `a parked read is answered by the poll that applies its offset, and only once` fails with two answers, you are answering before removing, or not removing at all.

drill.title: Write the waiting read from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `readAfter(account, offset, reply)` and the release step a poll runs after applying entries. Then write the one rule a client uses to apply pushed diffs safely.

recap: Indexes, replicas and materialized views are derived data a database maintains for you. Building one on a live table is snapshot, catch up, keep up: the same as bootstrapping a replica, a CDC snapshot or a kappa replay.
Unbundling moves that machinery out of the database: one log is the write path, and each derived store is a consumer running your derivation code.
Federation (Trino, foreign tables) unifies reads across stores. Unbundling keeps their writes in step, which is the harder problem. If one product does everything you need, use it.
The write path does work when data arrives; the read path when someone asks. A derived dataset is where they meet, and pushing diffs to clients extends the write path to the screen.
Pushed diffs carry offsets: a client applies only newer ones and resumes from its last offset after a reconnect.
Streaming databases (Materialize, RisingWave, Feldera) maintain SQL views incrementally, and they're still derived and behind. A read that needs its own write waits for the write's offset.

quiz.q: Support's OpenSearch index needs a new field on every payment document: the issuing country, looked up from the card's BIN. There are 40 million documents, and the index is fed from the payments topic. How do you add it?
options: Run an update-by-query on the live index that computes the field for every document
Build a new index with a consumer that runs the new code from the start of the topic (or from a snapshot), then switch the alias when it has caught up
Add the field to the consumer and let new payments fill it in over time
Write the field from the payments service directly, next to the topic
quiz.why: This is lesson 1's recipe applied to a search index: a new derived store, built by the new derivation code from the log, beside the old one, with readers switched when it has caught up. The alias switch is the atomic flip, and the old index stays for rollback. Updating in place mixes old and new documents for as long as it runs and leaves nothing to roll back to. Filling in over time leaves old payments without the field forever, and a direct write is a dual write.

quiz.q: Finance runs a Trino query that joins PostgreSQL's `payments` with the Iceberg `settlements` table. Someone suggests this means the warehouse no longer needs to be kept in sync with PostgreSQL. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: a federated query always sees both stores' latest data
Federation reads both stores as they are; it doesn't copy any change from one to the other
Trino can't read PostgreSQL
Trino caches results, so the join is always a day old
quiz.why: Federation unifies reads. The join sees PostgreSQL's rows and whatever the Iceberg table holds, and if the Iceberg table is missing yesterday's settlements, the query silently lacks them. Keeping the warehouse current is a write-side problem: a change log and a loader. The first option confuses "one query over both" with "both agree".

quiz.q: The merchant dashboard shows "takings today" and is refreshed by 2,000 merchants all day. An analyst also explores refund rates by any combination of country, card type and hour. Where should each workload's work go?
options: Both on the read path: compute everything when asked, so nothing is ever stale
Both on the write path: precompute every answer as payments arrive
The dashboard on the write path (maintain a per-merchant total); the analyst on the read path (scan when asked)
The dashboard on the read path; the analyst on the write path
quiz.why: The dashboard asks one question constantly, so paying a little on every write to make each read a lookup wins. The analyst's questions are many, different and rare, and precomputing every combination of filters is impossible, so they belong on the read path, against a store built for scans. Putting everything on the read path makes 2,000 merchants rerun the same SUM all day.

quiz.q: A merchant portal receives balance changes as deltas ("-45.00") over SSE. After a reconnect, the server replays the deltas since the client's last offset, and two deltas the client had already applied arrive again. The client doesn't track offsets. What does the merchant see?
options: The correct balance, because the server sends the same deltas
A balance off by the two repeated deltas, until the page is reloaded
An error, because SSE refuses duplicate events
The correct balance, because deltas are idempotent
quiz.why: A delta changes the value it's applied to, so applying it twice moves the balance twice. Deltas are not idempotent, which is why each diff carries its offset and the client drops any diff whose offset isn't above the last one it applied. A full value ("balance = 955.00") would survive a repeat, but it can still be overwritten by an older one arriving late, so it needs the offset too.

quiz.q: After a refund commits in PostgreSQL, the API reads the merchant's total from a RisingWave materialized view fed by CDC, and sometimes shows the old total. Which fix makes the API's own read always include the refund?
options: Run the refund transaction at SERIALIZABLE
Ask RisingWave to process changes faster
Return the refund's commit position and have the read wait until the view has applied it, or read this one value from PostgreSQL
Use a RisingWave subscription instead of a SELECT
quiz.why: The view is derived and receives the change asynchronously, so only a read that waits for the write's position, or goes to the system of record, is guaranteed to include it. A faster view makes stale reads rarer but not impossible, as the Try it shows at 10 ms. Serializable isolation governs transactions inside PostgreSQL and says nothing about a copy elsewhere. A subscription delivers the change soon after it's applied, which helps a screen catch up but doesn't stop the read that happens first.

flashcards.front: What three steps build any derived structure on live data?
flashcards.back: Take a snapshot, catch up on the changes made since the snapshot, then keep up with new ones. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, replica setup and CDC snapshots all do this.

flashcards.front: Federation or unbundling: which keeps stores in agreement?
flashcards.back: Unbundling: one log of writes, consumed by every derived store. Federation only lets one query read several stores as they are.
The application code that turns a change in the source into changes in a derived store, like building a search document or summing a window.
Write path: work done when data arrives, whether or not anyone asks. Read path: work done when someone asks. A derived dataset sits where they meet.

flashcards.front: Why must a pushed diff carry an offset?
flashcards.back: So the client can apply each diff once and in order, ignore repeats after a reconnect, and ask for everything after its last offset.

flashcards.front: How does a read get its own write from a derived view?
flashcards.back: The write returns its log offset (or LSN); the read waits until the view's applied offset reaches it, or reads the system of record instead.

terms.plain: Taking a database's derived-data machinery (indexes, views, replication) outside it: one log of writes feeding separate stores.
One query interface over several stores, such as Trino or a foreign data wrapper. It unifies reads, not writes.
Code that computes a derived record from source records.
Work done when data is written, and work done when it is read. Derived data moves work from the second to the first.
A message saying how one row of a view changed, with the log offset that caused it.
A database that keeps SQL views up to date incrementally from change streams, and can stream the view's changes out.
DBSP's change format: rows with integer weights, +1 for an insert and -1 for a delete.

explain_back.prompt: A product engineer asks why the portal sometimes shows a refund as missing right after the API said it succeeded, and whether switching the read model to a streaming database will fix it. Answer in your own words.
explain_back.answer: The API writes the refund to the system of record and returns as soon as that's durable. The portal reads from a read model, a copy that a consumer updates from the change log a few milliseconds to a few seconds later. A read in that gap gets the old value. A streaming database would maintain the same view with less code of ours, but it's still a copy fed asynchronously, so the gap is still there. The fix is to make the reads that need the refund say so: the API returns the refund's position in the log, and the portal's next read passes that position and waits until the read model has applied it, which is usually no wait at all and occasionally tens of milliseconds. For the live screen, we push each change with its offset, and the browser resumes from its last offset after a reconnect, so it never shows a change twice or misses one.

deeper.body:
**Spreadsheets did it first.** Change a cell in a spreadsheet and every formula that depends on it recomputes: a dataflow system on one machine, with no durability and no faults. Unbundling asks for that behaviour across many machines and teams, with crashes, ordering and replays handled, which is why it needs logs and offsets rather than a dependency graph in memory.

**Reads as events.** If read requests also go through the log, a read becomes a join between the request stream and the current state, and a subscription is a join that never ends. Logging reads costs I/O, but it records what each user saw when they made a decision: the shipping estimate shown before a purchase, the balance shown before a payout. Some fraud and audit systems do exactly this.

**Differential dataflow and DBSP.** Materialize's engine comes from Frank McSherry's work on differential dataflow, which represents every collection as changes over (possibly nested) time and computes outputs incrementally even for iterative queries. DBSP, which Feldera implements and McSherry co-authored, recasts the same goal as a small algebra over streams of Z-sets, with an algorithm that incrementalizes any program written in it. The paper shows SQL and Datalog both fit.

**Where this goes wrong.** Every stage in an unbundled system is another place for lag, bugs and schema drift, and there is no single `EXPLAIN` that shows the whole path. Teams that do it well keep a catalogue of which store derives from which, monitor lag per consumer as a first-class metric, and rehearse rebuilds.

The framing of unbundling, federation versus unbundling, and the write and read paths follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13; the CREATE INDEX observation is from the same chapter.
